name: XWind: A Cross-site Router for Large Language Model Inference Serving at Renewable Energy Farms
problem: AI power demand is growing while grids struggle to keep up; grid expansion carries high capital cost and transmission losses, yet abundant renewable energy exists at the source, just not matched to demand.
mechanism: Proposes 'AI Greeninferencing' - bringing modular AI compute to renewable energy sources (wind) to create behind-the-meter demand and ease strain on utilities - plus XWind, a lightweight reactive workload-agnostic inference router using only real-time signals (inference latency, KV-cache utilisation, queue depth) to configure sites and distribute requests under variable wind power.
speedup_reported: Reduces P99 end-to-end latency by up to 52% over the strongest contender - which is also the authors' own idea - and by up to 98% over baselines SUCH AS POWER-CAPPING AND GPU IDLING. Evaluated on a real 64-GPU A100 testbed emulating three wind-powered sites using Azure production traces, with consistent gains across workload types, load levels and GPU generations. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the 98% figure is against the authors' own chosen baselines, not against the absence of the technique, so it measures how much better routing is than static power management - it is not a general claim about cross-site routing performance.
notes: INCLUDED BECAUSE IT INVERTS THE USUAL SIGN AND IS THEREFORE A TRAP FOR THE READER WHO SKIMS. Power-capping and GPU idling are this paper's BASELINES TO BEAT, not its recommendations - so it should not be cited as evidence that power-capping is a good idea. Its actual distinctive contribution to this slice is geographic: it treats the interconnector and transmission constraint recorded in supply/grid-interconnection-queue-power-not-chips as something to engineer around by co-locating compute with generation, and its feasibility analysis asserts 890+ GW of wind capacity lies within 50 ms network round trip time of Azure data centers. That 50 ms figure is the operative constraint and is a latency budget, not a power figure - the interesting inversion is that a POWER problem gets solved by a NETWORK-LATENCY argument. Note the tension with supply/grid-interconnection-queue-power-not-chips: behind-the-meter co-location is precisely the case the LBNL dataset excludes from its queue statistics, which is why that record flags its scope limits so explicitly. Affiliations are unverified - the author list spans multiple organisations and no affiliation block was captured.
